text: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring with no repeating characters.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Substring means contiguous, not a subsequence. For a, b, c, a, b, c, b, b, it's three — a, b, c. For p, w, w, k, e, w, it's three — w, k, e. For five b's, it's one. An empty string returns zero. And the character set — letters, digits, symbols, spaces?
Yes, the full ASCII range, and n is up to five times ten to the fourth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would enumerate every substring and check it — quadratic or worse. This problem reminds me of a variable-length sliding window. I expand the right pointer, and whenever the window contains a duplicate, I shrink from the left until it's valid again, tracking the max window length. Both pointers only move forward, so it's linear. The contrast with a fixed-size window: there you shrink by size; here I shrink by validity.
What tells you the window is invalid?

A count map over the window. After adding the new character, only that character can have just become a duplicate — everything else was already unique. So I check whether its count is above one, and shrink until it drops back to one.

Here's the plan. One: left pointer at zero, empty count map. Two: for each right pointer, add its character to the map. Three: while that character's count is above one, drop the left end and move left forward; then update the max with the window length. One thing worth flagging — it's a while, not an if. The shrink isn't a fixed amount; it keeps going until the window is valid again. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop over the right pointer: count the new character in, shrink from the left while it's duplicated, then record the window length. The line that's easy to get wrong is the shrink — it has to be a while, because the old copy may sit several characters in. A faster variant stores each character's last index, so left jumps instead of stepping — same linear time, smaller constant. The key line there is the guard: only jump if that last index is still inside the window, at or after left.

Let's trace p, w, w, k, e, w — expected three. The row that matters is the second w, at index two. One shrink drops the p but leaves w, w, still invalid, so the while keeps going until the old w is out and the window is just w. At index four the window becomes w, k, e, so it returns three. That matches. Corner cases: an empty string — the loop never runs, zero. All the same character — one. And for the jump variant, a, b, b, a — the guard stops left from moving backward.
Why is the while loop still linear overall?
It's amortized. Left only advances, at most n times in total across all iterations. So it's the right pointer's n steps plus at most n steps for left — linear, not nested quadratic.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — each of the two pointers crosses the string once. Space is order k — the count map is bounded by the character set, at most a hundred and twenty-eight. Oh, one more thing — this same skeleton handles a whole family by swapping the validity condition. Allowing up to k replacements becomes window length minus the top count at most k. And shortest-window problems flip it to shrink while the window is still valid.
Great. You distinguished fixed and variable windows, justified the while and the amortized bound, and handled the last-index edge case. Done.
